When was that?

On March 23, 1910. What did these shares cost Mackenzie and Mann? They were issued to them for what? They manipulated 500,000 acres at $3 an acre. The reports they put in show that the land they bought from themselves cost $3 an acre in addition to the 100,000 acres they took for themselves first for nothing. Then, when they are hard up, when money is a little tight, they say: We will go to the milch cow, the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and sell to them stock for $12.50 a share, and that company paid them, according to this report, $483,000. In the light of that transaction, which is proved to the hilt, will any man for a single moment believe that these wizards of finance handled all this money all these years for nothing, that the Imperial Rolling Stock Company handled $32,000,000 merely for the sake of drawing their cheques? Go to the people of the country and tell them that these noble patriots, these splendid philanthropists, handled $200,000,000 for nothing, just for the satisfaction of the thing, just for the sake of writing their names and signing their cheques, and ask them to believe such a story. We may presume upon the credulity of the people to a certain extent, but if there is any man so credulous as to believe that statement he is unworthy to direct the law operations of the Crown. Now I shall leave that transaction.
I wish to say a word more about the Canadian Northern Express Company. The chief railway commissioner reduced the rates of that company because they showed an operating surplus of $152,000. They had padded the accounts in order to make this showing in anticipation of a bond

issue, and next year, when the surplus had been reduced to $48,000, Mr. Hanna said:	That is all right. Certainly, if you
pad your earnings up to $152,000 and then consent to a reduction to $48,000, you are easily satisfied. Then they tell us that these people made no money out of their telegraphs and they want the people of the country to believe it. These operations are all in line with the prairie land transaction -something for nothing; that is the motto, and the House and the country are asked to believe that these men handled these enormous sums of money day after day for nothing. It is the height of insanity to presume that the people of the country, with all their credulity, will, for a single moment, believe it. Now I have finished that phase of the matter.
These gentlemen, they say, are illy paid. They say that they have received nothing. They were contractors for the railway and they built it. At what price were they contractors? The Solicitor General says that they were not contractors in the proper sense of the term. Either they were or they were not. To whom were the cheques paid for the services .rendered? They drew the subsidies and they received them in the capacity of contractors or they had no right to them at all. It follows that these people fixed the prices which they themselves would get for their work. I do not know as to this, but I will give the Solicitor General and this House the benefit of some information I have and it is that eminent engineers, who worked for them and who are no longer in their employ, tell me that the prices that were given for handling rock and earth on the line between Kamloops and Victoria were forty per cent more than people would have put them at if they had been asked to tender.

I know it is official from the Department of Railways and Canals, but one of the most eminent engineers in charge of this work wrote me and told me personally that the work cost 40 per cent more than it could have been done for by tender and contract. Name a single contractor who was asked to tender for tills work. If tenders had been called for, this work would not have been in the position it is.
The same question arises too. in connection with the marketing and sale of these securities. I do not care as to what may be the observation of somebody in the Railway Department; the Railway Department work on the theory that the total cost will be so much and that so much has been done. That may be true, but when it comes down to taking section after section I say, lay upon the table of the House the price per yard that was paid for that work, then ask for competitive bids and let the people of Canada say whether the prices were fair or not. It is stated that these two men, in their capacity of contractors, have taken from themselves in their capacity as owners sums of money from 25 to 40 per cent more than the amount for which the work could have been done. We have the right to know whether this is true or not. I demand an inquiry under oath that we may know. You *may talk till kingdom come and you may say that somebody whispers this or that somebody tells you that, that the record shows this or the record shows that, but there is one record, the record that the people would like to have, and that is the record resulting from the opportunity of examining these men before a competent Canadian tribunal and finding out from them what the facts are. Since when has it been a crime to seek for information? Since when has it been a crime foT people to want to know what the facts are? Since when are the facts to be regarded as statements made by one of the parties to the issue? Has it come to this, in this free country, that the men who are on trial are to be believed though not on oath and that nobody else is to have a chance to say anything? I prefer to take the attitude of a

common layman, a highly cultured gentleman, the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) who was much more guarded in his statements this afternoon. He considered the evidence an)d found the contractors Mackenzie and Mann ' guilty.'
I say to my hon. friend the Solicitor General, do not, in the enthusiasm of your desire to serve the Government, be carried away in the defence of men whose nefarious transactions have made this Dominion a byword and the trail of whose corruptions extends from Victoria to Halifax.
We have been told that the stock of this company had been reduced by $45,000,000, but I shall show this House that such a statement is obviously untrue and absolutely false according to the records which have been brought down. If you will turn to page 34 of the blue book which has been distributed you will find that the sum total of the capitalization of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and of its auxiliaries was $145,000,000 and of that $145,000,000 there is already resting in the treasury of the Canadian Northern Company over $45,000,000 leaving outstanding a sum total of capitalization for the Canadian Northern railway and its subsidiaries and allied companies of $100,000,000. Of that $100,000,000 you will observe that $77,000,000 is now issued stock of the Canadian Northern proper, so that as I have already said, $23,000,000 of new stock is to be issued to enable the parent company to acquire and hold in its treasury $23,000,000 of useless watered stock of subsidiary and allied companies.
Who would not make such a deal? Let us look at the value of the $145,000,000. I started with the Bay of Quinte railway, and I pointed out, according to Poor's Railway Manual-and I gave the page to you this afternoon and I will repeat it- at page 1657, that road has had a deficit and has not paid its fixed charges since 1908. Yet these men have the hardihood and the effrontery to come to this Parliament and say that part of the floating liabilities of the Canadian Northern system is this $173,114.58 of the Bay of Quinte Railway Company, which represents the sum total of its accumulated deficits. This stock, which is subject to foreclosure and to be absolutely wiped out because the road is in default and not paying its fixed charges, is exchanged for over a million dollars of Canadian Northern stock. The voice is the voice of the Government, but the hand is the hand of Zebulon. That is all I can say. It is so obvious, so plain that he who runs may read. The idea of
saying that the stock of a company, which is in default under its securities, which may be foreclosed to-morrow and over which a receiver may be appointed, should be exchanged for over a million dollars of Canadian Northern stock is so absurd that it is surprising that a man would come to Parliament and ask any one to take it. Why? Because on the million dollars you ask the East and the West, and more particularly the West, to pay freight rates. If the evidence of Mr. Muller given before the Board of Railway Commissioners is correct, then that stock should earn $60,000 per annum, which means that that amount would have to be taken out of the farmers and grain growers of western Canada to pay interest as a fixed charge. Is it a reasonable thing to ask the people of Canada to pay $60,000 per annum on $1,395,000 of water in the Bay of Quinte railway, a railway which should be in the hands of a receiver and which has an accumulated deficit of $173,114.58?
We go to the next one-the Canadian Northern Alberta, alf page 1673 of Poor's Railway Manual. You will see that the issued capital stock is $3,000,000. Did it cost one dollar? No; it cost the price of lithographing the plate and grinding it off on the printing press. As I said this afternoon of the authors of the Canadian Northern system: Your greed is the only limit to your wealth, if you have a printing press a contracting and a railway company. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), who has known what it was in times past to vote against his party, knows that we in the West will have to pay, according to the economic theories that now prevail upon that $3,000,000 for all time a minimum of six per cent or $180,000 each year. This water is exchanged now, par for par, dollar for dollar, for Canadian Northern stock.
Then we go to the next-the Canadian Northern Western Railway Company. My hon. friend from Edmonton will bear me out-my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) knows that it was incorporated against our protest with a fictitious capital -a capital that represents all water. At the present time this railway company is building branch lines in the province of Alberta and has built a completed line to the Brazeau coal fields, which are controlled by a German syndicate and our friends Mackenzie and Mann. It is right and proper and fitting that these gentlemen should have interests in coal mines and other things as well. When this House

was told that these men were being fairly compensated! by common stock, because they had devoted their time and energies principally to the Canadian Northern railway, surely we overlooked the London Stock Exchange year book for 1914. There is nothing in which these gentlemen do not find scope for their activities or for the development of their splendid exploiting genius. As I said this afternoon, the fishes in the sea, the cattle on the hills, the timber on the plains, the splendid prairies, all pay toll to them, because whenever they saw something that seemed to be worth something, that would pay something; that it seemed possible to exploit with profit, these gentlemen were there for the purpose of exploiting it. I quote once more from the history of great railways to show the historical parallel:
* Year after year the interests of these men spread in many directions. They went into banking, politics, legislation, land-owning, navigation and newspapers; and with particularly unfortunate results to the public, went into street railroads. They increased their investments and power; and turned their profits made from one greedy enterprise into power to secure more greedy enterprises to gain more profits and more power.'
Those are not my words; they are the words of a great author describing conditions in the United States during and after the construction of the Central and Southern Pacific. Could words more aptly describe what has happened in this country?
Not content with putting the $3,000,000 of water into the Canadian Northern Alberta, they launched into the enterprise known as the Canadian Northern Western in connection with the Brazeau coal fields. They were able to induce this year, by that insidious* lobbying to which I shall again refer before I resume my seat, the legislature of the province of Alberta to guarantee the bonds of the Canadian Northern Western Railway Company to the Brazeau coal fields for $25,000 per mile at four and a half per cent, a completed road, after the bonds of this road guaranteed by the Canadian Northern had not been sold. It is in this enterprise, provincial in its character, local in its nature, intended for one purpose alone, that I am asked to see the people of Canada become partners-and I protest.
We go to the next line-the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company, dealt with in Poor's Railway Manual at page 1673. As this road is only in the construction stage, its inability to meet the fixed charges is what one might naturally expect; and during its construction, interest accounts are charged up against the 
proceeds of the bonds. Next year, when that road is completed, the fixed charges on it must be met. The Canadian Northern Ontario has a sweet story behind it. Let me tell you what the capital of that company was. According to Poor's Manual at page 1673, when this Parliament rose in 1912, the capital issued stock of the Canadian Northern Ontario was $250,000 of water. I will tell you how it was done: The directors of Mackenzie & Mann, Ltd., meet together as railway directors and say: We will give you all the stock and all the bonds, if you will build the road. Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann and Mr. Zebulon A. Lash said: We will make a little deal with ourselves as contractors, and you will have all the stock and all the bonds and all the monies if you will build the road. When you go to Parliament, there is no contract, you are merely financial agents, looking for money. So they issued the capital. Here is Poor's Railway Manual, page 1674, showing Canadian Northern Ontario's capital account in 1912 as $250,000, all paid up; but after last session, learning a lesson taught by the Parliament of Canada, they rushed to the printing press, and what do you think the capital is to-night-$10,000,000. And the capital stock of that road, which hon. members w'ill see from the statement amounted to a considerable sum, is to be handed to us to be exchanged for Canadian Northern stock. So much for the $100,000,000; so much for the reduction in the capital stock. I challenge any man in this House, in the face of these documents and in the face of the reports published in Poor's Railroad Manual, to say that we have reduced the capital stock of the Canadian Northern. On the contrary, what we have done I have just described. Sessional paper No. 269 c, which I think, is not printed, shows that the floating debt of the Canadian Northern Railway Company anu other allied companies amounts to over $10,000,000. The identities of these companies are to be preserved; their corporate existence is to be assured, but there is to be substituted for their stock-not, mark you, a substitution in the sense that there is to be an exchange, but the purchase price to be paid in respect of that stock by the treasury of the Canadian Northern railway is the difference between $77,000,000 and $100,000,000, $23,000,000. But that is not all. Did you ever hear tell of five per cent income charge convertible bonds? The genius of these men as financiers I do not desire to underestimate. There is no scheme known to the wit of man; there is no device that ever financial acumen knew of which they have not resorted fo. I desire to pay tribute to the colossal brain and intellect that is behind it all: that there is not in this great Dominion a man with the intellect, the keen perception and the financial acumen of Mr. Z. A. Lash. But his great powers of intellect and mind and his great legal knowledge are used for this corporation's advancement at the expense of the people of this country. And that is his business, mark you, but his viewpoint is constantly the viewpoint of a man who acts for the company of which he is a director, for the interests which he serves and serves so well. He has been able to create schemes and systems that almost, but not quite, dazzle the intellect, confuse the mind and prevent their being understood. These five per cent convertible

bonds that were issued from time to time amounted to $25,000,000. The first issue was $7,500,000; the second issue was $7,500,000 and the next was $10,000,000. When the first block was put on the London market, they sold at less than par. When the next block was put on the London market, they sold for less than par. When the last block was placed on the London market, by a clever system of financing indicated in a special letter which was sent to a syndicate of which the British Empire Trust Company was a part, of which Mr. Horne Payne is the managing director and of which Sir William Mackenzie is also a director; the British Empire Trust Company and a few men in high finance in London conceived the possibility of taking an option from the first upon this convertible stock in order that they might be able to sell it at more than par. And so, according to the prospectus I have under my hand under which these bonds were launched upon the London market, they w?ere placed at 106 and the premium amounted to $600,000, of which $250,000 only found its way into the coffers of the Canadian Northern. At least, the report says so; perhaps everything is not told in the report, but it says that that is all the railways put in. They issued a prospectus in which they stated to the people who invested, that this rioad would soon he another Canadian Pacific and the English investors bought at 106 these convertible certificates, payins a premium of $600,000. When they issued the trust deed under which these bonds were secured, the capital stock of the company was only $55,000,000. I commend the attention of the House to this paragraph in exhibit No. 269a, the trust deed for the five per cent convertible stock. These are the words:
And whereas the company represents that the capital stock of the company is now $70,000,000, divided into shares of common stock of $100 each, of which $55,000,000 has been issued and is outstanding and fully paid up.
$70,000,000 authorized, $55,000,000 outstanding and income certificates tobeissued amounting to $15,000,000. It was necessary, as these were convertible, to put into the hands of the trustees $15,000,000 worth of stock. It is stated, as I pointed out, in the prospectus that as this company's stock in the first instance had not been increased and was only $55,000,000, it would be necessary to increase the capital to $70,000,000. . They increased the capital; they put the $15,000,000 up and now they want us to do it over again, because in this
agreement the right is reserved to this company to increase its capital to another $25,000,000. My friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) yesterday directed attention to that point. So not only was the capital increased from $55,000,000 to $70,000,000 between June 30,. 1909, and June 30, 1910; not only was there $15,000,000 not issued on May 6, 1910, the date of the trust deed, but the $15,000,000 having been deposited for the purpose which I have stated, it looks to be an easy chance to do the people again, and so we take the right to add another $25,000,000 to the capital whereby the capital becomes $125,000,000 although, according to the trust deed, $15,000,000 of that has already been taken care of. But Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann say: oh, no, we did not take care of that; all we did was this: we put our stock up with the trustees only in the meantime and until the opportune time came to change it for treasury stock. Now is the opportune time, they say. Evidently they believe in the old doctrine: 'now is the appointed time.'
The hon. Solicitor General told us, as did other members who spoke on the subject, and as did the hon. member for St. Antoine, that we were going to get security upon these various debentures and stocks mentioned in the second part of the second schedule. Why, Sir, we have them now. The company has borrowed all the money it could upon them by debenture stock issues, and these are not redeemable. The stock is irredeemable and perpetual. Why fool us with stories like that?
Why tell us there is equity in something that is mortgaged for all time, perpetual, irredeemable? What does perpetual mean if not irredeemable, for all time? Can they talk about an equity of redemption in a perpetual stock? That is a contradiction of terms, an abuse of language. The fact is that the securities are held in perpetuity by the Trust company for the four per cent perpetual debenture stock and in the prospectus on which they were sold these words appeared:
This stock is perpetual and irredeemable.
Then we pass on to the next point. The agreement has been said to involve absolutely a reduction of stock, and an improvement in our security. There is another thing said about this agreement that I should like to discuss. They say: We are getting forty per cent of the stock of this company and you should 'be satisfied; and we are going to get one director and a right to look at the

books and make an inspection and as my hon. friend besides me says, to have a balance sheet. That is a large concession. According to my appreciation of the Railway Act, railway companies have to render balance sheets anyway, but perhaps I am mistaken. In the facts I have stated as to how this capital is made up, as to how it has been constituted, the people of this country want no such partnership as that for their guarantee. You ask me why. Well, the fact is that one director can do nothing but create trouble. Do you realize that on the railway in Quebec to which I referred the city of Quebec had the right to name a director and the Government has a director on the board of the Grand Trunk Pacific even as the old Government of Canada had on the Grand Trank Board. I have heard of the enormous control exercised over the line. I have heard how he has cut down the cost of construction and reduced the cost of betterments! My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) will know what ia stupendous power the Government director on the Grand Trunk Pacific was in connection with that enterprise. There is only one thing for us to do, we must not permit the men who have created this condition to control and dominate and operate this road. One director is to add insult to the injury that has already been done to the Canadian people. I do not want any man representing me, as one citizen of this country, to sit at the board of this company and become a recording machine for a brute majority. What power would he have? He would have tire power to look at the books. According to my understanding of the law, any director may look at the books; and we have an absolute right, through the machinery of the Railway Act, to know about these things. The Government now says that we are going to have the right to look into the books, to inspect them, and to put a director on the board of an enterprise that bias been cursed with incompetency in operation, with inefficiency in upkeep, that is not a railway in a proper sense of the term-and we are to become partners in that and have one nuan on the board and a look in at the books. Why, Sir, it is monstrous, absolutely.
You may say that any man can be destructive in criticism and ask me what I offer against that. That is a fair question.
I offer this: I say that the stock
9 p.m. of that company should not be in the hands either of the Govern-

meni or of these men, that it should be in the hands of a trust company; and I would put a man in charge of the operation and completion of the construction of that road who was a railway man and not a contractor. Is it right that men occupying the dual capacity of owners and contractors should carry forward an enterprise on which they have brought disaster? I ask my hon. friend, would he do it in his business? Is there any man in this House who would do it in his own business? Would any reasonable business man in this House for a single moment entrust the administration of his estate and affairs to a man who had so mismanaged it as to bring about the crisis that now exists? The.first thing you would do would be to remove the incompetent servant or manager. care for the race that comes after us and not damn them and place them in a

The next distinctive feature referred to by my hon. friend this afternoon, and one which has been much relied upon by others, is the power of foreclosure. That upon the happening of any event of default and at any time or times while the same shall continue, it shall be lawful for the Governor in Council after such notice to the Canadian Northern as the Governor in Council may direct, to declare to be vacant the offices of the directors of the Canadian Northern, and to appoint a board or boards of directors in lieu thereof.

Semi-ready foreclosure.

I beseech hon. gentlemen with all the power I have to look at clause 24:
That if authorized by the Parliament of Canada, the Governor in Council may on such terms and conditions (if any) as Parliament may prescribe, at any time while any event of default shall exist and be continuing, by order declare the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern and of all other persons whomsoever in the mortgaged premises to be foreclosed, and thereupon the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern (and of such other persons) in the mortgaged premises and every part thereof shall he and become absolutely barred and foreclosed.
They talk about the slow machinery of the courts, hut look at this:	' That if

That is absurd. Let me read once more from the book to which I have already referred. The chapter and verse are indifferent, but the sentiment is important. It is speaking of the lobby Huntington carried on. You know the United States guaranteed the bonds of Huntington's road at 6 per cent and he got a land grant besides. The money cost, of course, was great, but as the cost was saddled directly upon the people, this was not a matter of importance to the company. It was equipped with funds to buy whatever was needed, and it had very active support in ways and from men that cost little or nothing.
This at first seems strange, hut on reflection will he found to be true and to represent a universal condition in this country. The railroad company took and still takes advantage of the following elements that exist in every community:
1.	Men that can be fooled by party loyalty.

Beyond these remains the class that must he
secured with money, including bosses, heelers, professional politicians, repeaters, colonizers, floaters, lodging-house keepers, the keepers of such dives and disorderly houses as cannot be controlled through the police, the saloon keepers that cannot be controlled through the breweries.
All of these were fully utilized by the polit-

ical department and secured for the railroad company through the control of the state legislature.
Now I ask that wo think of those words when we are considering the provision of this Act which will lead to one of the greatest lobbies ever known. I have had some experience in the practice of my profession and it has been my privilege, sometimes my unhappy lot, to foreclose mortgages, and sometimes under trust deeds.
Sometimes I have gone to the courts, when an appearance has been entered in behalf of those who orwn the property. Here these gentleman are putting up a claim and we are the mortgagees in possession responsible more strictly than in any other capacity that possibly could be created. I need not say to any lawyer in this House that a mortgagee in possession is held to more strict account than: any other man in the world. But that is not all. During the 'Course of my study of this matter I tried to ascertain what, thirty years ago, the Parliament of Canada did. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), with his forty years' experience, will remember what it did and it will be no new story that I repeat to him. ' I regret that we have not been able to sell our stock, although its dividends have been guaranteed by the Parliament

Is Sir William Mackenzie a less rich man than was Sir George Stephen? Are Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann less rich than Duncan McIntyre and Donald Smith of that day? There are men who say the richest man in Canada is Sir William Mackenzie. Why does he not lend something to his own enterprise? . I commend this House to the consideration of that letter of Sir George Stephen, now Lord Mount-Stephen. What did this Parliament do then about foreclosure? Let us look at the sections of the Act. The arrangement with the Canadian Pacific railway will be found in the statutes of 1884, chapter 1. This is now nothing more perhaps than a reminiscence; but is known that the caucus of that day rejected the proposals of Sir John Macdonald in the first instance to aid the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, but later on a modified proposal met with the approval of the caucus and it was enacted into law. There follows a statement as to what is to be done. Then, they are to build the line within a certain time and here is the section providing for the default, subsection 2 of section 6:
That upon default for twelve months in the payment of any half-yearly instalment of interest upon the said loan, or any part thereof, or of interest upon the said sum of seven million three hundred and eight thousand nine hundred and twelve dollars, or any part thereof, or in the payment of the principal of either of the said sums or any part of either of them when the same shall become due, in accordance with the provisions hereof, the right of the company under their contract hereinbefore mentioned, to demand or receive any further cash or land subsidy shall cease and determine, and the said railway and extensions thereof, branches, equipment, rolling stock, plant, including steamers, and all lands and property of the company and all land grant bonds then in the possession of the Government-

-shall vest in Her Majesty, and shall forthwith, thereupon, be taken possession of by the Minister of Railways and Canals, on behalf of the Government of Canada; and each and every employee of the company shall, from and after the expiry of the said period of twelve months, become and he the employee of the Government during pleasure, and shall hold and possess any matter or thing apertaining to the said company then in his custody, as and for the Government; and the rates of interest, and the terms of payment, hereby fixed, shall not be disturbed or altered by the terms of such agreement.
Then it goes on further:
The said company Is hereby authorized to execute an agreement of the nature and purport hereinbefore provided for, and to charge its entire property and assets, in manner and form as hereinbefore described; and in such agreement to agree upon such further and other conditions as the Government may prescribe; provided, that authority to the board of directors of the company to accept the provisions of this Act and to execute an agreement containing the charges upon the said railway and property and the other conditions required or authorized by this Act, shall be granted by the shareholders of the company, either by a resolution passed at a special general meeting of such shareholders called for the purpose, by a vote of at least two-thirds in value of such of the shareholders as shall be present or represented at such meeting, or by an instrument or instruments executed by at least two-thirds in value of the whole of the shareholders of the company, in person or represented by their attorneys or proxies, respectively, duly authorized in that behalf.
What does that mean ? That means that the shareholders agreed that their interest in the property as shareholders must, and

should be, lost, if they failed as shareholders to make good the conditions mentioned in the statute. What have we here? [DOT]-not any such thing as immediate foreclosure, and not any agreement by the shareholders by which their stocks may be forfeited. But having regard to the decisions of the Privy Council in cases that came from the province of Nova Scotia, it has been clearly and definitely stated and laid down that, unless the Crown states positively beyond question that it intends to destroy that which belongs to the private individual, as far as possible it shall not he destroyed without -adequate compensation. This $60,000,000 of stock, that may be scattered broadcast throughout the world, will stand at the door of Parliament and say: We paid eighty cents on the dollar for it when we bought it. It is true there is a statute, but we did not know about the statute; and because we did not know, we ask Parliament to listen to the greatest lobbying of our time and to postpone foreclosure until Parliament has passed and settled the terms. I ask the Government to adopt the terms of the Canadian Pacific statute and I say: If you are going on with this, then do not let Parliament again be disgraced by that which is referred to, in the history of the Huntingdon lobby, as the worst of its time. I am weary and sad to see the men who wander around and threaten and cajole and coax, and sometimes do one thing and sometimes another, in order to get us to do what they want. We are not here to discharge a public trust for this set of men or for any other set of men that may ever arise; and when we say that these men ought to be foreclosed,
I ask that they be foreclosed as it is provided that the Canadian Pacific railway may be foreclosed, namely, by a contract arranged between the shareholders and the Crown, by which the shareholders will say that,	if	default he made, thestock will be	wiped	out. Do	not
let us wait a year and permit this thing to happen. If you must do this thing, please do it at least in the manner I have mentioned-my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) says if they make default, then the axe will fall. It is not the axe; it was only the invitation that will be sent out- the invitation to an execution that might never take place; that might be postponed, and, after all, instead of being -an execution, might turn into a wedding.
One word more in relation to the question of interchanging traffic. Great credit was taken by the Administration because it said: We are going to have an interchange 
of traffic-and the statement did not contain the words 'as far -as possible.' I w-as taught to believe, in the school of law in which I had my training, that 'as far as possible' was always understood; -and, if you are going to say that a man who ships his goods cannot choose the route by which he is going to ship them, -something new has happened in -Canada. It surely is not contended by this Parliament that a man who ships his goods from Calgary cannot say: I am going to ship them via lake and rail, or via so-and-so or so-and-so. Surely it is not contended that you are going arbitrarily to say to every shipper in Canada: You must make a contract to ship your goods by such and such a railroad. If a shipper sees fit to choose a certain route, why, of course, by the Railway Act, he has the right to do so. I suppose you are going to amend the Railway Act -and declare that hereafter no shipper, at any point served by the Canadian Northern, will have the right to choose the route by which he shall ship his goods after they reach a point which may he served by one of the roads in the agreement. That is all there is in- it, and I leave the matter for th-e consideration of the House.
The question that is of vital importance to our country is the duplication of existing transportation facilities. I hold in my hand the judgment of the Board of Railway Commissioners in the western freight rate,? case. Might I offer this suggestion to the Government, that they have this document printed and distributed to every member of this Parliament, because, while there may be on the board men who differ from me, I would like to say this for the board, that it has expended an amount of industry -and care and patience and attention to the details of the transportation problem that -will astound those who take the trouble to read through theix report. I find on looking at this report that Mr. Drayton, at great length, at pages 53, 54 an-d 55, d-eal-s with the question of transportation facilities in Alberta and Saskatchewan, and alludes to the need for facilities that will serve the territory within ten miles of either side of the railways. He finally turns to the consideration raised by Mr. 'Muller, the expert, and points out that the real difficulty that has to be met is the question of the duplication of transportation -facilities. At pages 54, 55, 56 and 60 he deals with the whole question, and finally concludes as follows at page 67:
For the reasons already pointed out, the board, does not pass any opinion as to how

much of the duplication shown was or was not necessary. The criticism of Mr. Pitbiado, however, is at least in part well founded, and the necessity for a business control by the Government which will prevent the unnecessary duplication of transportation facilities in the future as urged by Mr. Bicknell, is established.
There I rest again. No provision in that regard has been made in this agreement. These men may continue, as they have been doing in days gone by, to push work out here and there, to get the bonds guaranteed, the bonds sold, the proceeds paid into the bank, and year after year no facilities created, year after year the time gone by and no road built. They give us facilities that parallel existing ones, and give the people no better transportation opportunities, because there can be no lessening of the rates, they being fixed by the Railway Commission. Where rates are fixed by the Railway Commission and are uniform, the duplication of existing transportation facilities is one of the worst grievances the people of the West have to contend against. I ask: Has any man looked into the transportation problem of western Canada in the light of existing conditions? You have the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, built to a standard never before seen on this continent, with eighty pound steel rails, with splendid grades and easy curves, a great artery capable of handling great traffic, but with few branch lines. Then you have the branch lines of the Canadian Northern scattered here and there, that might be made tributary to a great artery; and by some working agreement between these two systems, you might prevent the duplication of existing lines and offer to the people some effective transportation facilities. There is the opportunity. This $45,000,000 that we talk about so glibly to-day, wit hthe present cost of transportation, would give to western Canada thousands of miles of cheap roads. What we want is branch lines-surface roads, if you will-cheap feeders to great arteries, in order that the traffic of this country may be carried to the seaboard at a small cost. Mr. Drayton, in the judgment to which I have referred, points out that the cost to the farmer of getting his product to the railway is what destroys his profit. He points out that the cost is enormous- 20 cents a bushel in some instances, more than that in others. You will find it all dealt with at length between pages 50 and 60 of the judgment. It shows what is demanded is transportation facilities within ten miles
of the farmer that will enable him to get his crop to the market, whether it be cattle, or pigs, or butter, or eggs, or dairy produce, or wheat, or whatever it may be, so that he may be afforded the opportunity of getting the products of the soil and the produce of his toil carried to the markets of the world cheaply. This is what the West demands. This is what the Canadian Northern has failed to do. Its promoters have given vague promises-promises that have not been kept. They have made promises marked in black upon maps, which were calculated to mislead and which did mislead intending settlers.
North of the city of Edmonton there is a great fertile empire that is now being developed; and if the facilities now under construction are completed, there is a duplication, and the money so expended will not be used in giving to other sections of that vast empire the facilities that it so much requires and demands. That is the case in the province of Alberta and in the province of Saskatchewan, perhaps less so in the province of Manitoba; but what we require and demand is some policy of vigorous construction that will make possible the bringing of transporation facilities to the men who are building this empire.
That is what we demand, that is what we require. This partnership will not do. Since when did the loyalty of this country, since when did the intelligence of this country, permit the Crown to enter into partnership with men guilty of the misrepresentation of which we were the victims last session and which I have mentioned. Something was said of national disgrace. Certainly, it would be a national disgrace for the Crown to enter into partnership with the men from whom we have obtained $7,000,000 of watered stock ground out by the printing press. That was taken at two hundred cents on the dollar. It had a high value last year. This year, of course, the price is less. We get the $33,000,000 more and are giving a guarantee to pay $45,000,000 and putting ourselves behind over $200,000,000 besides. I guess the stock is going down, or up-but nobody can tell unless it were a receiver or mortgagee in possession. But are we warranted in going into such partnership? I say, nay.
In conclusion:
1.	We have been in times past the victims of base deception;
2.	The reports published abroad by this company of its undertakings, its payments and receipts are apparently untrue, be-

cause the payments alleged are not shown to have been made, and moneys claimed to be on hand are now said not to be there.
3.	TMe stocks of the companies it is proposed to bring into this system are in many cases already partially held by the Canadian Northern railway, and the securities are now held in their entirety. These things are plain and obvious.
4.	By the alleged reduction of capital,
it is proposed to give life and vitality so far as can be given to water by this legislative action-to exchange stock that has no value for that which, according to the eminent authority whom we heard last evening will shortly reach par value. Imagine, for instance, $1,395,000 par value of Bay of Quinte stock being exchanged for shares of an equal value in the Canadian Northern railway to be, in a few years, worth par!	.
5.	We become mortgagee, receivers in possession, without any adequate provision for immediate foreclosure.
5. We become mortgagee-receivers in the people of the West will secure better or cheaper transportation facilities.
7. And lastly, it means a partnership which, for the reasons I have given, we cannot tolerate.
Then, you say, what do you offer in place of this arrangement? I answer at once: Instead of what is here proposed, first, the stock of this company should be vested in a trust company. Second, these men should be removed from their position of direction of an enterprise they have made insolvent. Third, a statute should be passed to enable the Governor in Council to advance money to pay the artisans, the contractors, the equipment builders-the men whose money and labour are in the enterprise and to subrogate us to the rights they have against the men with whom they have contracted-the Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited.
Then, I ask that we should make the fullest possible inquiry as to the condition of this road. There is a difference of opinion on that subject. The enterprise of these men may be surrounded with the halo which was pictured for us this afternoon. They may be the most slandered men in the world; they may be angels in, disguise. They are said to be poor men who left their native towns with little and are now worth millions; and it may be that these millions came to them even as the manna came from Heaven. It may be that this represents their honest toil as railway contractors to which for eighteen years they have given

their time. This may all be. If so there are no men so much interested in having it known as they. And it is necessary that the people of this country should know and understand, for we are to put ourselves as fourth mortgagees behind an enterprise of waterlogged securities and watered stock, and we demand that we should know what the end will be before we enter upon an undertaking so vast, a policy so hazardous.
But more-and with this I conclude. We ask that an opportunity be given to those who toil to get the produce of their land, the product of their toil, to the market at the least expense. My hon. friend from Kingston gave me great joy as he spoke last evening of the wants of the West and of the bond which lies between the Bast and the West: I ventured, at various Canadian clubs in this eastern country when first I came here, to point out some of the grievances, or alleged grievances, under which the people of the West labour. They complain of many things, but nothing strikes them so hard, nothing pinches them so cruelly, as undue railway tolls-the twenty cents a bushel that must go to get the crop to the railway on which there is but little profit. Nothing makes them more disconsolate, more unsettled and more discontented, than to think that the produce of their lands and their hands has gone merely to carry that produce to where it may be sold. We hope to develop the West.
I am an optimist; and I believe that in the West we have the greatest land under the British Crown potentially. But it requires strong hands, vigorous minds, great enthusiasm, much optimism, the expenditure of Capital, and beyond all that, a common feeling for a United Canada, to build in that West a great land. That is not going to be done rapidly; our population is not so easily to be assimilated. Here to-night upon this issue rests largely the future of the West. When they tell me what this road is going to earn, I refer to the figures, and I have under my hand a volume on the earning power of railways. Neither Mr. Hanna nor anybody else can tell me that they are going to earn fixed charges with the traffic that it will be possible for them to develop. They know it, I know it, the country knows	it.	Shall we, then,
take this road and operate it as a Government enterprise? I cannot say until we have had a report and physical valuation. The people of the United 'States have found that freight rates must be based on

physical valuation-that water has no value. That physical valuation will show what the property is worth. The long ten-years' struggle in the United States came to an end last year, and the Inter-State Commerce Commission commenced its labour of physically valuing every road in the United States, and on that valuation they will base the freight rates of the country. Let us begin right. We aire putting upon the people of western Canada especially a burden. Let us pause before we go forward lest it be said of us that we have made progress too swift and have not considered the end from the beginning. They are the statesmen, who in public affairs forecast every phase of a proposed policy and understand what it means. It is for us to look at this enterprise in that way, and not to he deterred from our duty because the action which that duty lays upon us seems temporarily unpopular.
iSir, I have to thank the members of this House for the patience with which they have listened to me. What this poet said with regard to empire builders seems to me to be strictly applicable to this situation in view of the contention that has from time to time been heralded abroad that wre should be generous to Mackenzie and Mann as empire builders:
Who are the Empire-builders?
They whose desperate arrogance demands A self-reflecting power to sway A hundred little selfless lands?
Lord God of battle, ere we bow To these and to their soulless lust,
Let fall thy thunders on us now And strike us equal to the dust.
Leaders unknown of hopes forlorn Go past us in the daily mart With many a shadowy crown of thorn And many a kingly broken heart;

We only see its cross is red

Aye, and their brother-men forget
The simple wounds in palm and side.
But he that to his home is true,
Where'ere the tides of power may flow,

think that the hon. member who has just sat down is entitled to be congratulated on the independence of spirit which he has shown and the House is indebted to him for the study which he has given to the very important subject that is now under discussion. I am not. altogether able to agree with the view that he expressed in the beginning of his remarks, however, that this Canadian Northern enterprise was beyond the scope and necessities of the Dominion of Canada. He strongly took the ground that Canada is not big enough for three transcontinental railways. I will admit that, but we want three transcontinental railways to make Canada bigger; we think that is one of the ways by which Canada's greatness may be advanced. As to the possibilities, let me point out that there are to-day three railways from Chicago by way of St. Paul to Puget Sound passing through a territory absolutely similar to that in our country between Winnipeg and the coast, absolutely similar and of like extent, and that these three railways find great business, large traffic and satisfactory profits from the carrying of freight and passengers through the tier of states that lie alongside the Canadian boundary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What are the roads to which my hon. friend refers ?

The Northern Pacific, the Great Northern and the Chicago, Milwaukee and Puget Sound. I say that what has been done south of the boundary can be done north of the boundary, and that what has been necessary south of the boundary is or will be necessary north of the boundary. I note that when the right hon. Prime Minister was making his presentation of this case he took occasion to remind the House that it was the Liberal Government, by their action in 1911, that committed Canada to the Canadian Northern system as a transcontinental enterprise. I think I saw in the allusion something more than the desire to give credit to the late Liberal Government. I am rather of the view that



the right hon. Prime Minister was laying the foundation for the argument that such difficulties as surround the Government of the day in dealing, with the Canadian Northern are measurably due to the late Government, and that for them the present Government is not entirely responsible. For what the late Government did the late Government must assume the responsibility, and I believe the members of that Government are entirely willing to assume full responsibility for everything that they did in connection with this Canadian Northern enterprise, as well as with regard to other matters. But while they are prepared to assume full responsibility for what they did, let there be a sharp distinction drawn between what they did and what they did not do: between the responsibilities of the late Government and the responsibilities of the present Government, which began in the fall of 1911, two and a half years ago. It is true that the Liberal Government gave important aid to the schemes of railway transportation that now constitute the Canadian Northern system, and it is true that in the year 1911, when they made provision by guarantee for connection of the eastern with the western sections of that system, they did use the argument that a transcontinental system was desirable. But let me point this out: that while they said then, and I say now, that a third transcontinental railway system such as that undertaken by the Canadian Northern is an ultimate necessity for this Dominion of Canada, it does not by any means follow that it was then or is now an immediate or pressing necessity. Let me make my point clear. The Canadian Northern, as the House has already been informed, had its inception in the province of Manitoba as a local project. It was then extended to connect the province of Manitoba with lake Superior. That having been done, a guarantee was given by the Liberal Government to enable the company to extend its lines from Grandview, in Manitoba, to Edmonton, and from the Manitoba boundary to Prince Albert, a guarantee of $13,000 a mile for the respective distances, some six hundred miles in one case and two hundred miles in the other. These lines were built. Following upon their construction the provincial Governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta saw fit to make provision for extensions of branch lines from the main line for the accommodation of the people of those provinces, for their greater	development, and	for the
[Mr Oliver.]
benefit and welfare of the Dominion of Canada. A great transportation system was built up in those western provinces, extending from lake Superior practically to the Rocky mountains, on the joint responsibility of the Dominion and of the three prairie provinces. At the same time enterprises were entered npon in the eastern provinces by the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and by 1911 railroad connections had been established under control of the Canadian Northern railway between the cities of Quebec, Montreal and Ottawa, and between Toronto and Sudbury. For reasons that have been given to the House, it seemed to the Government of that day desirable that the important commercial and industrial centres of eastern Canada touched by the Canadian Northern railway should be directly connected with the system of the same company operating in the three prairie provinces, so that, on the one hand, that .system operating in the prairie provinces would have independent and competitive access to the eastern seaboard and the eastern commercial centres, and, on the other hand, that these commercial centres should have direct, independent and competitive access to the prairie West. That action by the Liberal Government of that day has been condemned by the Solicitor General. As a member of that Government, I have no apology to offer for the action that was taken, for the purpose of the action or for its result. It was a necessity of the case arising out of conditions as they had been created. It was essentially for the welfare of eastern and western Canada, and to bind eastern and western Canada in a common interest as they could not have been so thoroughly bound without it. It may have been that the enterprise could have been delayed for a year or two years, but, at any rate, under the conditions as they then were, that part of the project was favoured by the late Government, and to-day the rails are connected between Toronto and Winnipeg, and are within measurable distance of being connected between Montreal and Winnipeg. Had the enterprise been confined to the area between the city of Quebec and the foot of the Rocky mountains, as it was confined so far as the assistance given by the late Liberal Government is concerned, there would not have been facing this Government and this country to-day that condition which has been characterized here as

a railroad, as a financial, and, as it may develop, possibly a political crisis.
No danger of that.

While we give this company all credit for enterprise it is possible for this or any other company to be enterprising beyond the limits of good business, and it is perfectly clear to-day that it is owing to the fact that this company undertook to establish its connection from the prairies to the Pacific ocean before it had - established and built up a pro-
10 p.m. Stable connection between the prairies and the eastern seaboard that the difficulties of this company and of this Government have arisen and for that condition this Government must take its full share of responsibility. When Mackenzie and Mann or the Canadian Northern Railway came to the late Government and said: We want to have a transcontinental line, we want to build through British Columbia, we have the guarantee of the British Columbia Government, and we want assistance from you to enable us to complete our line through British Columbia to the Pacific coast, they were specifically and definitely refused that assistance, and until the present Government came into power their expenditures upon that part of the project were of a minor character. But as soon as this Government came into power, the first session of Parliament saw a demand by the Canadian Northern Railway for $6,000,000 to be used in building from the Yellowhead Pass to Vancouver, and it was given to them without a question, without a condition of any kind. It was this Government that committed the people of Canada to the building of that part of the transcontinental line prematurely and because of that commitment, for which this Government must take the responsibility, the Canadian Northern railway and the Government and the country find themselves in difficulties to-day. Up to the present time there has been expended, according to the return, a matter of some thirty odd million dollars upon that section of the road. It still calls for an expenditure of $23,000,000 to complete, a matter of approximately $60,000,000 required for the British Columbia section of this enterprise. All that the company requires to borrow, so it says, is $45,000,000. If it had not undertaken to carry that load of the extension through British Columbia before the time was ripe, this difficulty would not have arisen. For this difficulty the Government must take the full re-2384
sponsibility and cannot lay any portion of it upon the late Government.
I do not wish to weary the House by traversing the terms of the resolutions, as they have already been dealt with so fully, but I do say that when a serious financial situation came up for consideration, when the credit of the country and its welfare were seriously concerned, when the matter had tc come before Parliament, it was a most unfortunate thing "that there should have been sent broadcast throughout the country, upon the stated authority of this Government, an absolute misrepresentation of the facts in regard to the resolutions to be submitted to the House. It is most unfortunate that this should have taken place. The night the resolutions were brought down there was put upon the wires-it must be presumed with the authority of the Government-a series of statements in regard to these resolutions that are not borne out by the facts. There was a statement that $15,000,000 worth of the stock of the Canadian Northern was to be placed in trust to become the property of the Government in order to give them control of the stock of the -company in case of default. There is no such provision in the resolutions.
That was in the Liberal press.

The Conservative press.
That statement was made in an editorial of the Ottawa Journal this week.
You put too much stock in the Liberal press.

I do not wish to get entangled in an argument with my hon. friend, tout that is a childish suggestion). This statement went on the Associated Press wires, and it went out, I take it, on the authority of the Solicitor General.

I think I can be excused for interrupting now. It did not go out with my authority, either directly or indirectly. I never heard of it until I read, it in the newspapers, nor do I think it went out on the authority of any member of the Government.

It is a fact that it went

The public have not had the benefit of seeing the resolutions in the press. It is a most unfortunate thing, I repeat, that this rank misrepresentation should have been sent out in regard to this very important matter. I make this allusion for the purpose of bringing the point home, that when our friends opposite find they are criticised in regard to the subject matter of these resolutions for not having acted, apparently, in good faith they must blame [DOT] themselves, or their friends, because they have already prejudiced the court of public opinion against them.
The particular feature that I wish to bring to the attention of the House, however, in connection with these resolutions is following up certain questions that I placed before the Prime Minister some days ago. I desired to have the information as a -basis for the views I had to place place before the House in regard to the resolutions. However, this is the aspect of the question to which I wish to draw special attention, and which, except for a side remark by the Solicitor General, has not been dealt with in any way in the discussion up to -date. I have already said that the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and other provinces, have joined with the Dominion Government in- carrying forward the Canadian Northern railway enterprise by guaranteeing the bonds of branch lines. This is a matter of intense importance to the people of those provinces and to their governments. I need not spend time in explaining the situation. We have there a
[Mr. Oliver..!
vast area of country into which population rushed at a most unprecedented rate. Those Settlers scattered all over the great provinces, were in absolute need of railroad communication. Although the responsibility for providing that railroad communication properly rested upon the Dominion Governments the Dominion Government felt that it was doing all that it was warranted to d-o in providing the main lines of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the (provincial governments therefore either had to take measures to provide further railroad communication, or settlement in those provinces would have come to a standstill or retrogressed. For good and sufficient reasons, those provinces have guaranteed the bonds of branch lines of the Canadian Northern to the extent of many millions of dollars, and of many hundreds of miles of railway. I am interested in knowing on behalf of those provinces what part the interests, there existing, are to have in the project under the impetus given to it by the proposed guarantee. In the province of Alberta some 1,400 miles of line have been guaranteed. The guarantees amount to about $22,000,000. Some 500 miles have been- constructed, some 200 miles are under construction and some 400 oir 500 miles still remain guaranteed but to be constructed. I am a member of the Parliament of Canada and I am called upon to vote to give the Canadian Northern Railway Company a guarantee of $45,000,000. It is, of course, interesting to me what the security is going to be, what the terms are going to be, but it is very much more interesting to me to know how far, and to what extent, the completion of the branch line enterprise, undertaken in the provinces of Alberta -and Saskatchewan, is going to be promoted by the vote I give. If I am to vote $45,000,000 to the Canadian Northern Railway Company and if the people I represent are to be left without the railway communication that they have been expecting to get from the Canadian Northern Railway Company, I will not be here in the next Parliament; that can be taken for granted. I want to know very definitely, for my own information, but still more in the interests of these provincial governments, how far this -proposed aid is going to promote the railway enterprises in these provinces which these provinces have guaranteed and whose completion is an -absolute necessity for the further development of these provinces and for the welfare of the

people already occupying the laud. Men who are from the West know perfectly well that when a line has been laid out, a guarantee given and a part of the line constructed, people have occupied the country for the whole length of the proposed line in the full confidence and expectation that the line would be completed. Work on a number of these lines has been at a standstill during the last two summers. The people have been told: the company is hard up, they cannot raise the money, you cannot get the line. But if the company is going to get $45,000,000 at the hands of this Government, the people will want to know why these lines are not completed; and that is what I want to know from the Government.
They will not build branch lines with that.
Then, if they do not, I certainly would isay that they cannot have my vote for the loan.
Your view is very sectional.

Well, I will have to stand the criticism. I 'was elected to represent the people in the part of the country from which I come and I am bound to represent them in this House. I was under the impression that that was what Parliament was for. However, I will have to accept the criticism.
There is another question I want to discuss with the Government in this connection. I notice that the resolutions make provision that a very considerable amo.unt of money that is owing by the Canadian Northern Railway Company is not to be paid out of this $45,000,000. I have listened to the discussion and I must say that I view the matter from a different angle from that from which it is viewed by some hon. gentlemen. I do not know why this Parliament is voting money unless it is to see that the money that is owing by the company is paid. It seems to me that this is the very first purpose to which this money ought to be devoted. I am at a loss to understand the reason behind the arrangement that especially stipulates that some $15,000,000 or $20,000,000 which is said to be owing to-day by this company is not to be provided for out of this money that is being voted by Parliament. If bills are owing in that part of the country from which I come, certainly the creditors will want to know why they do not get paid
377f
if Parliament has voted the money. I cannot understand the reasoning which caused the agreement to be so drawn as to provide that the money to be voted is not to be used to pay accounts that are already due.
Does my hon. friend think they will not be paid?

I do not know whether
they will be paid or not.
They are not to be paid out of the $45,000,000.

If they are not to be paid out of the money the hon. member (Mr. Blain) and myself are voting, if we have' voted the money on the understanding that it will not be used for the payment of these debts, and if, perchance, they are not paid, I want to know what we will say to those to whom that money is owing.
What would likely happen if the Parliament and Government of Canada refused to help them?

That is not the question that is before the House. That is a matter that we would be quite willing to take up and consider in other circumstances, but we are dealing with a proposal to ask Parliament to guarantee $45,000,000 in aid of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I cannot understand how, if the Canadian Northern Railway Company need that money to pay their debts, it should not be used for the purpose of paying their debts. If they are insolvent, if they cannot pay, are these people to be left without their money? If they are not insolvent why are they owing that money to-day?
I want to know to what purpose this money is going to be devoted. Is it going to be used to pay the debts of the company, and is it to be used to complete the project now undertaken on the responsibility of the provincial Governments of the prairie provinces? In my constituency there is a settlement in the grand prairie of the Peace river. It is 200 miles from the nearest railway point. Some eight or ten townships there have been settled. The Canadian Northern have a line projected for a distance of 300 miles from Edmonton. They have a guarantee from the provincial Government of 100 miles. They have built some forty miles, and have laid steel. They have done grading on the balance, I believe, of the 100 miles. I certainly want to know whether that 100 miles is to be completed or not.
Agility.

Yes, and agility-he was arguing with great cleverness that a third or fourth mortgage on what he himself has given to be understood was a presently bankrupt institution, was a more valid security than a first mortgage on the same identical project. He set himself a heavy task, and I must say he acquitted himself with credit; yet I do not think he quite proved his point.
This resolution is difficult to deal with. It has been the occasion of a great deal of eloquence both to-day and yesterday, and I do not think that the subject is exhausted by any means. I have given the matter some study, and my conclusion is that this resolution is a purposely involved attempt to establish a controlling junior partnership with an insolvent debtor. It is not remarkable if such an attempt should lead to difficulty in demonstrating absolutely what is meant by what is said.
I object to this resolution because it is improvident, and it is improvident because it is inefficient. What is the purpose of this aid that we are giving? It is to preserve the credit of the country, to secure the completion of the system and to insure the permanence of the Canadian Northern as a competitive railway system. Are any of these purposes served under the terms of the resolution? The credit of the country is not preserved-provision is made that the money that we provide shall not be used to pay the company's debts; their debts are still to be left unpaid. Will this money that is to be voted complete the system? The claim was made last year that the $15,000,000 of cash that we then voted

would secure the completion of the system. But it did not, and there is no more reason to-day, on the showing that has been placed before the House, to believe that the $45,000,000 will secure the completion of the system than there was to believe that the $15,000,000 of last year would secure its completion. With $58,000,000 to raise on securities not yet earned, it is a grave question if the money can be secured to complete the system. But our hon. friends say that they have security on everything that the company has, and that they have made provision for taking over the company's belongings. Is it for the sake of the security that they are advancing this money? I fancy that if it were merely for the security, they could advance the money for other purposes and get much better security. They are advancing the money to prevent the system from going into bankruptcy and to secure its permanence, and when they have advanced the money they will have not one dollar's worth more of valid security than they have to-day, before they advance the money. That, I think, has been demonstrated to-day. All the security that they will have when they have put this marvellously and wonderfully-worded resolution into effect; all the security they will have of any value, they have to-day. This resolution is merely a form of words to cover up the fact that the Government are advancing $45,000,000 to the Canadian Northern, without security, to enable the company to avoid bankruptcy. A year from now, when the money has been spent and the $58,000,000 that is expected to be raised has not been raised, and the company is again unable to pay its debts, every reason that my hon. friend has given for not foreclosing the mortgage that we have on the Canadian Northern to-day will exist then, reinforced by the amount of money that we have voted in the meantime. To-day we do not dare to foreclose, because the company owes too much money; yet we give them $45,000,000 more, and we are going to foreclose if they are not then in a position to carry on the enterprise. Surely if we are not going to foreclose now, when we have put $45,000,000 more into the enterprise, we are not going to foreclose then.

The hon. gentleman argues as if he were of the opinion that we should foreclose now. Is that the state of the hon. gentleman's mind?

I am not giving my opinion at the present time; I will deal with that later. I am arguing on this point, and I would like the hon. gentleman's careful attention to it. It is this: we to-day hold a first mortgage on the Canadian Northern enterprise in its most important parts. We can foreclose that mortgage to-day if we see fit, but we do not want to do it. Why? Because of the reasons that have been given to the House. We are going to give the company $45,000,000 and we are not going to be in any better position when we have given that $45,000,000 than we are now. We cannot foreclose any quicker and if we will not foreclose now, are we going to foreclose then? I say, certainly not. The whole of this resolution is for the purpose of exchanging a preferred creditorship for a junior partnership in a practically defaulting enterprise. I am not saying that that is not necessary in the interests of the country; I am not arguing either one way or the other. What I am arguing is that this Government has absolutely deceived or attempted to deceive the public in regard to their position towards this company and with regard to the result of the action that is to be taken. They have told Parliament and they have told the country that they arc getting security when, as they have been informed this afternoon, they are actually increasing their, liability without increasing their security.

Do you think that as
well?
Mr. OLIVER; I do not merely think it; I know it. Does my hon. friend not know it?
Indeed I do not.

I am not of the legal profession, but I think that that is elementary and that even I can demonstrate it. There is to-day on the line from Grand View to Edmonton a first mortgage held by this Government for $13,000 a mile. Superimposed upon that are certain bonds issued by the Canadian Northern-I do not know how much a mile, but I venture to say that they covered everything they could get. Upon that my* hon. friend is going to superimpose another mortgage as security for this $45,000,000. Supposing the company defaults and he forecloses; how is he going to collect his equity of redemption in the mortgage that he is putting on now if he does not assume responsibility for the second mortgage that the Canadian Northern have given on that road?

Well, my hon. friend will not admit anything?

I misunderstood what
the hon. gentleman said first. There is no doubt at all that by the present resolutions we incur greater liability. What .1 thought the hon. gentleman said was that by taking, the other companies in we had not added to our security and had added to our liability. I was not dealing with
that. Now that my hon. friend has mentioned the taking in of the other companies, 1 may say that I heard several speakers here to-day and yesterday declare that the stock of these subsidiary companies has been reduced; that the water has been squeezed out of these companies. That is the way, at any rate, the pdblic were given to understand the matter; that this Gov-* ernment had driven a hard bargain with Mackenzie and Mann; that they had put them right up against the wall and had taken these stocks from them, squeezed the water out of them and reduced everything down to a basis of $100,000,01)0. Now, is there any foundation for that statement ? Absolutely none whatever. What is the idea of watering stock? It is that there shall be shares of stock which shall draw dividends, if dividends there be, and if you reduce the number of the shares then there will be a lesser number to draw dividends on. Take the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway with its $10,000,000 of stock. Suppose the Canadian Northern Ontario railway earns dividends a year from now or ten years from now, will it be paying dividends on anything less than $10,000,000 of stock? Not one cent less. It is true -that the Canadian Northern railway will get the benefit of the dividends, but the dividends will be paid on $10,000,000 of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway stock, and so right along the line. I would be sorry to accuse our hon. friends of intentionally misleading; they may have believed when they made the statement that they were actually squeezing water our of this stock. This resolution states that it is to be increased to $100,000,000 and that difference is .to be handed over to Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann; and yet they have sent the statement throughout all Canada that they had decreased the stock of the Canadian Northern railway. It is not $100,000,000 it is $125,000,000. I maintain that this proposal should either be a loan on terms that, failing substantial security, wrould ensure proper expenditure of the money in payment of indebtedness and completion of the enterprise, or a definite, controlling interest in the company.

That covenants or undertakings of the contractors and such other covenants or undertakings as may he required by the Governor in Council shall be given that the current indebtedness of the Canadian Northern and of the said constituent and subsidiary companies will within one year from the passing of the Act to be based upon these resolutions be reduced to the normal or usual current amount to be determined by the minister and that meanwhile all such current indebtedness other than such as may be the subject of bona fide dispute, will be either paid or arranged in such a manner that no proceedings for the enforcement of payment thereof will be taken or pressed.
Who gives the covenant?

The contractors give undertakings that they will reduce the current indebtedness to an amount to be fixed by the minister. Now Mackenzie and Mann, it is said, are not able to pay their debts to-day; that is why they are here, and yet we are taking a covenant from them that they will pay their debts if we give them this money.

Mr.' OLIVER: I maintain that if this resolution has a pui*pose at all, it is to see that the debts of the company are paid, and it is not making that provision; it is to see that the enterprises of the company are completed, and it is not making that provision; it is to see that the property of the company, in case of default, becomes the property of the people of Canada, and it is not making that provision; in none of these particulars does it meet the requirements of the case. I object to these resolutions because they establish a junior, partnership with an insolvent debtor. They, in effect, compel further aid to prevent future bankruptcy. While professing to take security they establish a largely increased liability. Although they lay an enormous additional burden on the credit of the country they do not provide for outstanding liabilities. They do not secure completion of the enterprise; they do not protect provincial interests; they do not provide for minimum freight rates; and in case of foreclosure, they do not provide for Government ownership of the property.
